title: CIBC Presents: Eyes on Velocity: How AI Is Changing the Fundraising Equation
description: An investor and lender panel on AI, growth, productivity and the requirements for funding. Moderator: Falon O'Keefe.

summary.overview: What makes an AI company financeable when software can be built faster and copied more easily? Investors and lenders from Pelorus, The51, BDC and venture lending discussed how their decisions are changing. Across different funding stages and instruments, the panel returned to capable management, evidence of customer demand, resilient differentiation and the ability to adapt. Sarah Murphy of Pelorus emphasized early founder learning and speed; Shelley Kuipers of The51 highlighted distribution, community and business-model resilience; Brian Whiteway of BDC emphasized differentiated data and the right capital for each stage; and Eric Laflamme discussed how lenders evaluate investor support and whether established software businesses can defend their positions.

keyTakeaways.heading: At the earliest stage, speed of learning can matter more than a moat
keyTakeaways.explanation: Sarah Murphy said she does not expect a pre-seed prototype to be impossible to copy. She looks for founders who test assumptions rapidly, detect where customers respond and follow that evidence into a stronger opportunity. She gave an example of a founder testing many ideas in a matter of weeks before concentrating on one with market pull.

keyTakeaways.heading: AI makes distribution, data and execution more defensible
keyTakeaways.explanation: Shelley Kuipers emphasized networks, customers, community and distribution when a product can be reproduced. Brian Whiteway pointed to proprietary data, including examples of patterns visible only when information from multiple financial institutions is combined. Technology still matters, but a generic interface over widely accessible AI is not much of a competitive advantage by itself.

keyTakeaways.heading: Investors want the difficult conversation early
keyTakeaways.explanation: Across the panel, funders repeatedly called transparency a positive sign. They want founders to share problems, uncertainties and deviations from forecasts early enough to help. A management team that can admit it does not know the answer, learn and adapt may inspire more confidence than one that claims certainty.

detailedSummary.heading: Different funding tools for different companies
paragraphs: The panellists represented distinct parts of the financing landscape. Sarah Murphy described Pelorus's focus on early-stage, venture-scale Newfoundland and Labrador companies. Shelley Kuipers described The51's investment network and its focus on women-led innovation, particularly around health, wealth and work. Brian Whiteway outlined BDC's range of support, including patient growth and transition capital for businesses between traditional lending and venture financing. Eric Laflamme described venture lending for high-growth companies with institutional investors behind them.

A recurring point was that the right amount and kind of financing depends on the problem being solved. Whiteway urged founders to start with the business need, rather than announcing that they require a particular multimillion-dollar sum. Laflamme said venture debt adds financing alongside committed equity backing; it is not a substitute for having sufficient liquidity and investors willing to support the company.

detailedSummary.heading: How funders judge the people building the business
paragraphs: Murphy said an important early signal is how founders respond when their first plans fail: whether they can acknowledge reality and rapidly find another route. Whiteway similarly prioritized aligned, capable management, arguing that an adaptive team can be more valuable than excellent technology without the ability to execute.

Kuipers discussed whether The51 could contribute more than money through its community, expertise and distribution relationships. Fit runs both ways: an investor must be the right partner for the business. The discussion made clear that venture-scale ambition is not the same as the financing needs of every profitable small or medium-sized company.

detailedSummary.heading: What becomes defensible when building gets cheaper
paragraphs: Kuipers argued that network effects, communities, distribution and durable customer relationships can distinguish companies whose underlying AI-enabled software can be reproduced. Whiteway stressed the role of proprietary information that a competitor cannot simply obtain from public sources, using aggregated financial-institution data as an example of insights unavailable to an individual data holder.

Laflamme described examining AI from both a defensive perspective—how an established company uses it to improve operations—and an offensive perspective—whether new competitors can threaten its business. He noted that mature systems embedded in customer processes may have switching costs and existing relationships that pure newcomers cannot instantly replicate. However, complacency remains dangerous.

detailedSummary.heading: Velocity and market evidence at pre-seed
paragraphs: Murphy distinguished the earliest investment stage from later defensibility tests. She described evaluating how quickly a team learns, experiments and engages customers. A product's first version may be easily replicated, but founders can use rapid feedback to develop a distinct position over time.

Her example involved a team abandoning an initial direction, running many small experiments and concentrating on the one attracting meaningful interest. The importance was not the raw number of tests but the willingness to follow evidence rather than defend an original idea.

detailedSummary.heading: Trust, communication and helping when things go wrong
paragraphs: Multiple panellists described proactive communication as an essential investor relationship. Murphy wants founders to call when something goes wrong rather than wait until a crisis is unavoidable. Whiteway values leaders willing to admit uncertainty, because doing so creates a more useful conversation about possible responses.

Kuipers explained how investor networks can mobilize people with practical experience, not only capital. Laflamme made a distinction between equity and lending: a lender expects repayment and needs early warning when growth, liquidity or loan conditions may be at risk. The more time a funding partner has, the more options may remain available.

detailedSummary.heading: A financing decision is also a partnership decision
paragraphs: The discussion closed by stressing fit and collaboration among investors. The financial backers on a company's cap table can make introductions, advise management and coordinate help through difficult periods; poorly aligned investors can create friction.

The panellists encouraged founders to engage the local startup community and learn from other teams. The message was that financing is more than one cheque: capital, counsel, time, relationships and the team's willingness to learn all affect the company's prospects.

highlightedInsight.heading: Learning velocity is an investable capability
highlightedInsight.explanation: Murphy's early-stage distinction is particularly useful for AI founders: a prototype can be copied, but the capacity to conduct experiments, interpret customer reactions and pursue a better market opportunity is a capability that can compound.

notableIdeas: Equity and debt providers evaluate different risks: upside and long-term value versus the capacity for repayment.
Some mature software businesses may retain defensibility through embedded systems, customer relationships and differentiated data.
Funders described founder transparency about setbacks as a signal of strength, not an automatic loss of confidence.
practicalApplications: Before seeking capital, define what specifically needs funding, how the spending changes the company's prospects and why that funding instrument fits.
Document what customers do rather than only what they say; use experiments to demonstrate learning velocity.
Identify defensibility beyond code, such as proprietary data, customer access, distribution, expertise or switching costs.
Give financing partners early, candid updates about missed assumptions and ask for advice while options remain open.
